newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil CenBank blamed for undermining Bamerindus.
newsitem.headline: Brazil CenBank blamed for undermining Bamerindus.

text.p: The former majority shareholder of Brazil's fourth largest private bank Bamerindus blamed the Central Bank for leaking misleading information which undermined the bank's performance, spurring its takeover by HSBC last week.

In an interview with O Globo newspaper published on Monday, former majority shareholder Senator Jose Eduardo Andrade Vieira denied that Bamerindus was facing problems in 1995, saying the bank even posted a net profit of 100 million reais ($94.3 million) in the first half of that year.

"Bamerindus was healthy. It was the group which faced problems with debt," Vieira told O Globo, referring to once-sprawling holdings of the Bamerindus conglomerate, including such diverse subsidiaries as a paper mill and an insurance company.
"The problem was that the Central Bank leaked versions that Bamerindus was having difficulties and from then on the bank started to lose deposits."
Vieira in the newspaper interview provided no further details on the purported central bank leaks.

Bamerindus, which was suffering from market rumors and press reports of liquidity problems since 1995 and losing 50 million reais ($47.2 million) a month, was taken over by Hong Kong Shanghai Bank Holdings Plc (HSBC) last week.
Vieira said the central bank finalized the HSBC takeover of Bamerindus without consulting him.
Vieira said he has contracted Rio de Janeiro lawyer Jose Luiz Bulhoes Pedreira and he did not rule out court action on the takeover.
"There is no rush to file a lawsuit," Vieira told O Globo. "The idea is to get as much information as possible and then decide what to do."

He said the Bamerindus takeover was an "exceptional" deal for HSBC, which bought up 10 billion reais ($9.4 billion) worth of healthy Bamerindus assets in return for a $1 billion capital injection into a new bank which opens Monday as Banco HSBC Bamerindus SA.

Vieira said a financially healthy Bamerindus was worth 1.5 billion reais ($1.4 billion), but HSBC had only paid the Central Bank $400 million given that "HSBC paid the $1 billion in Brazilian foreign debt paper that is worth 40 percent of its face value".
((--Simona de Logu, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 507 4151))
